passed.title: is_duplicated flags every copy, not just the repeats after the first
passed.trap: Pandas `duplicated()` defaults to `keep='first'`, so it flags only the later copies. `Series.is_duplicated` flags **every** occurrence of a value that appears more than once, including the first. Filtering with `~s.is_duplicated()` therefore drops all copies of a repeated value; it does not deduplicate. To match pandas `keep='first'`, use `~Series.is_first_distinct()`. To match `keep='last'`, use `~Series.is_last_distinct()`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [1, 2, 2, 3, 2])

# Wrong: flags the first 2 as well
print(s.is_duplicated().to_list())
# Wrong dedup: every copy of 2 disappears
print(s.filter(~s.is_duplicated()).to_list())

# Right: pandas keep='first' semantics
print((~s.is_first_distinct()).to_list())
# Right dedup that keeps the first occurrence
print(s.filter(s.is_first_distinct()).to_list())
passed.output:
[False, True, True, False, True]
[1, 3]
[False, False, True, False, True]
[1, 2, 3]

passed.title: NaN and null are different: fill_null and is_null ignore NaN
passed.trap: Unlike pandas, Polars keeps the missing value (null) separate from the float NaN. `Series.fill_null` leaves NaN untouched, and `Series.fill_nan` leaves nulls untouched. `Series.is_null` returns `False` for NaN, and `Series.is_nan` returns null (not `False`) for a null element. To clean both, convert NaN to null first with `s.fill_nan(None)`, then call `Series.fill_null`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("x", [1.0, None, float("nan")])

print(s.fill_null(0.0).to_list())  # NaN survives
print(s.fill_nan(0.0).to_list())   # null survives
print(s.is_null().to_list())       # NaN not flagged
print(s.is_nan().to_list())

# Right: turn NaN into null, then fill all missing values at once
print(s.fill_nan(None).fill_null(0.0).to_list())
passed.output:
[1.0, 0.0, nan]
[1.0, None, 0.0]
[False, True, False]
[False, None, True]
[1.0, 0.0, 0.0]

passed.title: is_in returns null for null inputs unless nulls_equal=True
passed.trap: With the default `nulls_equal=False`, `Series.is_in` returns null (not `False`) for null elements. Negating the mask leaves that null in place, and `Series.filter` discards null mask positions. So a null row vanishes from both the "in" result and the "not in" result. Pass `nulls_equal=True` to treat null as an ordinary value. A null that is not in `other` then yields `False`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("b", [2, 4, None])

m = s.is_in([1, 2, 3])
print(m.to_list())                 # [True, False, None]
print(s.filter(~m).to_list())      # null row silently lost

m2 = s.is_in([1, 2, 3], nulls_equal=True)
print(m2.to_list())                # [True, False, False]
print(s.filter(~m2).to_list())     # null row kept in the complement

passed.title: filter drops rows where the mask is null, so mask and ~mask do not partition the data
passed.trap: `Series.filter` keeps only positions where the predicate is `True`. Positions where it is null are discarded. A comparison such as `Series.gt` on data containing nulls returns null at those positions. That means `s.filter(mask)` and `s.filter(~mask)` together lose the null rows. Decide explicitly where nulls belong by calling `fill_null(True)` or `fill_null(False)` on the mask.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [10, None, 30])
mask = s.gt(15)
print(mask.to_list())                       # [False, None, True]

print(s.filter(mask).to_list())             # [30]
print(s.filter(~mask).to_list())            # [10]  -> null row in neither

# Right: decide where nulls go
print(s.filter(mask.fill_null(False)).to_list())
print(s.filter((~mask).fill_null(True)).to_list())

passed.title: is_between includes both bounds by default and never swaps reversed bounds
passed.trap: `Series.is_between` defaults to `closed='both'`, like SQL `BETWEEN`. If you build adjacent buckets with it, values that sit exactly on a shared edge are counted in two buckets. Use `closed='left'` or `closed='right'` for half-open bins. If `lower_bound` is greater than `upper_bound`, the bounds are not swapped and the result is all `False`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("num", [1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

# Wrong: 3 lands in both buckets
print(s.is_between(1, 3).sum(), s.is_between(3, 5).sum())  # 3 3 -> 6 of 5 values

# Right: half-open buckets
print(s.is_between(1, 3, closed="left").sum(), s.is_between(3, 5).sum())

# Reversed bounds give all False
print(s.is_between(4, 2).to_list())

passed.title: interpolate leaves edge nulls and changes integers to Float64
passed.trap: `Series.interpolate` and `Series.interpolate_by` only fill nulls that lie between two known values. Leading and trailing nulls remain null, so do not assume the result is null-free. Linear interpolation of an integer Series returns `Float64`, as the docstring example shows. Handle the edges explicitly, for example with `Series.forward_fill` and `backward_fill`, and cast back if you need integers.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [None, 1, None, 3, None])
r = s.interpolate()
print(r.dtype)
print(r.to_list())                     # edges are still null
print(r.null_count())

filled = r.forward_fill().backward_fill()
print(filled.to_list())
print(filled.cast(pl.Int64).to_list())

passed.title: index_of returns None when not found, and index 0 is falsy
passed.trap: `Series.index_of` returns the position of the first match, or `None` when the value is absent. It does not return `-1` and it does not raise like pandas `get_loc`. A truthiness check such as `if s.index_of(v):` therefore reports "not found" for a match at index 0. Always compare with `is not None`. Passing `None` searches for the first null.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [17, None, 5])

idx = s.index_of(17)
print(idx)                              # 0
print("truthy check:", bool(idx))       # False -> wrongly 'not found'
print("correct check:", idx is not None)

print(s.index_of(55))                   # None, not -1
print(s.index_of(None))                 # 1, position of the null
passed.output:
0
truthy check: False
correct check: True
None
1

passed.title: has_validity is deprecated; has_nulls replaces it and ignores NaN
passed.trap: `Series.has_validity` has been deprecated since 0.20.30. Use `Series.has_nulls` instead. `Series.has_nulls` only reports null values, so a float Series full of NaN still returns `False`. To detect NaN, use `Series.is_nan` combined with `any()`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

f = pl.Series("x", [1.0, float("nan")])
print(f.has_nulls())          # False, despite the NaN
print(f.is_nan().any())       # True

g = pl.Series("y", [1.0, None])
print(g.has_nulls())          # True
print(g.null_count())
